course.title: Camday – Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics — Stage 8

unit.title: Collecting Data
unit.blurb: Planning a statistical investigation: types of data, questionnaires, data-collection sheets, populations and samples.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Plan an investigation: choose the data to collect, classify data, and design questionnaires and data-collection sheets.

O2.t: Understand populations and samples, choose a sample size and recognise how sampling can introduce bias.

lesson.t: How do I plan a statistical investigation?
p: Write a clear question or **hypothesis** to test (e.g. 'Students who read more spell better').
Decide **what data** you need, **where** it comes from and **how much**.
**Primary data** you collect yourself (survey, experiment, observation). **Secondary data** was collected by someone else (internet, books, records).

lesson.t: What kinds of data are there?
p: **Categorical (qualitative)**: words or groups – favourite subject.
**Discrete**: numbers that are counted and take separate values – number of pets.
**Continuous**: numbers that are measured and can take any value in a range – height, mass, time.

lesson.t: How do I write good questionnaire questions?
p: A good question is **clear**, **not leading** (it does not push towards one answer) and has **response boxes** that cover every answer **without overlapping**.
Bad: 'Don't you agree that homework is too long?' (leading). Bad boxes: 0–1 h, 1–2 h (1 h is in both).
Good: 'How long do you spend on homework each night?' □ less than 1 h □ 1 h up to 2 h □ 2 h or more.

lesson.t: How do I design a data-collection sheet?
p: Step 1: List the categories or groups (non-overlapping, covering everything).
Step 2: Add a tally column.
Step 3: Add a frequency column.
Step 4: Add a total to check the count.

lesson.q: Classify: (a) hours of sleep, (b) number of brothers, (c) eye colour.
'How much TV do you watch? □ 0–2 h □ 2–4 h □ 4–6 h.' Give two problems.
steps: 2 h and 4 h each fit two boxes
More than 6 h has no box; no time period (per day? week?)
lesson.a: Overlapping boxes, no box over 6 h, and no time period

p: Questions that suggest an answer ('Don't you think…?') give biased results.
Test your response boxes: can every possible answer go in exactly one box?

p: The **population** is the whole group you want to know about. A **sample** is part of it.
We use samples because they are **quicker and cheaper**, and testing everything may be impossible (e.g. testing every battery until it runs out would leave none to sell).

lesson.t: How big should a sample be?
p: Larger samples are more **reliable**, but cost more time. A common choice is around **10%** of a population, and not fewer than about 30 if possible.
A school of 650 students: a 10% sample is 65 students.
**Bias** means the sample does not represent the population, so results are unfair.
Causes: asking only one group (only your friends), a sample too small, leading questions, or choosing people at a time or place that favours certain answers.
A **random sample** gives every member an equal chance (e.g. numbering everyone and using random numbers).

lesson.t: How do I choose a random sample?
p: Step 1: Number every member of the population.
Step 2: Use a random number generator (or names from a hat) to pick numbers.
Step 3: Ignore repeats until you have the sample size you need.

lesson.q: A factory makes 2400 bolts a day. A 5% sample is checked. How many bolts is that?
To find out how much exercise adults do, Lee asks people leaving a gym. Explain why this is biased.
steps: People at a gym exercise more than average
lesson.a: The sample over-represents people who exercise a lot; it is not random.

lesson.t: A big sample can still be biased
p: Asking 500 people at a gym is still biased. Fair selection matters as much as size.
When explaining bias, say which part of the population is under- or over-represented.
